title: Patara: yarn, trade and temple craft
description: Patara history in Odisha through yarn trading, historical weaving groups, silk procession ropes and Gamha Purnima craft in Puri.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: A finished cloth tells only part of the story of silk. Yarn must be supplied, threads prepared and skills passed on. Patara histories also lead into particular temple services, where silk becomes a procession rope or a carefully layered ceremonial thread.

paragraphs.text: The Bhadrak District Gazetteer describes Pataras dealing in silk and cotton yarn, stringing necklaces and supplying materials for weaving. Its examples include reeled yarn, hand-spun tussar and silk, borders and appliqué designs. This places the community’s recorded work across several stages of production and trade, rather than only at the loom.

The same account records devotion to Balabhadra and worship of working implements on Gamha Purnima, the full moon of Shrabana. The tools of livelihood enter the religious calendar. This is a district account, however, not evidence that every Patara household follows an identical observance.

In 1909, Edgar Thurston, assisted by K. Rangachari, described two Oriya Patrā sections: makers of silk waist-threads and tassels, and weavers of silk cloth. He recorded different offices for the two: a Mahanayako headed the cloth-weaving section, while a Senapati, assisted by a Dhanapati, headed the other. The account concerns community organisation as well as products.

These are colonial-era descriptions, not a present-day authority on identity. The book separately discusses Telugu Patras in Cuddapah and Kurnool; the similar name does not establish the same community. Nor do the recorded offices explain when or why the Odisha community first formed.
paragraphs.locator: VolumeVI printed177–178; distinction and editorial limits

paragraphs.text: At Puri, a specific service gives the history a different scale: the hands of a maker. Arunika Mohapatra’s 2017 report identifies patara servitors preparing silk Bijaya Dori for the pahandi procession of Jagannath and Balabhadra, using silk from Nuapatna. Interviewed maker Santosh Kumar Patra described tearing the silk by hand and estimating measurements by eye, without scissors, needles or scales.
paragraphs.locator: 2017 original reporting; pataras and Santosh interview

paragraphs.text: The report describes fathers and grandfathers teaching younger men. It also distinguishes these silk procession ropes from the chariot-pulling ropes supplied by the Odisha Coir Board. Remembering that difference helps us understand the particular skill being described. These servitors cannot stand for every member of the wider community.
paragraphs.locator: 2017 original reporting; family transmission and rope distinction

paragraphs.text: A different object requires a different method. Reporting in August 2026, Bratati Baral described Patara Bisoi servitors making the temple’s rakhis at home for Gamha Purnima. The temple administration supplied Vasunga silk. The makers dyed it, dried it in the sun and shaped circular layers, arranging five layers with a wooden comb before tying them with silk threads.

This named service gives a concrete local context for ceremonial threads in Odisha. It does not date the beginning of the practice or establish that every form of present-day Raksha Bandhan celebration has the same history.
paragraphs.locator: Editorial interpretation and limits of dated report

paragraphs.text: The records explain work, organisation and particular services; they do not identify one founder or founding date. Settlement and family histories remain to be investigated. A surname or an occupation in silk is not enough to identify someone’s caste.
